hook: A few rabbits released in Australia in 1859 had no foxes or diseases to hold them back and a whole continent of grass ahead of them. Within a few decades there were hundreds of millions. In a fenced field, the same rabbits would grow fast at first and then level off as grass and space ran short. Same animal, two growth curves: the J and the S.

options: The largest population an environment can support over time
The fastest a population can grow
The number of species in an area
The age when a species first breeds
prereq.why: Carrying capacity (K) is set by an environment’s resources.

prereq.q: A population grows 7% a year. About how long does it take to double, by the rule of 70?
prereq.why: 70 divided by the growth rate in percent: 70 / 7 = 10 years.

figure.caption: Exponential growth (J-curve) with unlimited resources, and logistic growth (S-curve) that levels off at the carrying capacity.

chain.cause: Resources are plentiful and nothing limits a population
chain.effect: it grows by a constant percent each year, so it adds more individuals each year: exponential growth, a J-curve

chain.cause: The population grows and resources are shared among more individuals
chain.effect: limiting factors such as food, space and disease become stronger

chain.cause: Births fall and deaths rise as the population nears carrying capacity
chain.effect: growth slows and the population levels off at K: logistic growth, an S-curve

ideas: Exponential growth: with unlimited resources, a population grows by a constant percent each period, so it adds more individuals each time. The graph is a J-curve.
Logistic growth: growth is fast at first, slows as resources run short, and levels off at the carrying capacity. The graph is an S-curve; growth is fastest at about half of K.
A limiting factor is any resource or condition that keeps a population from growing: food, water, space, light, nutrients, predators, disease.

Density-dependent factors grow stronger as a population gets denser (food shortage, disease, competition, predation). Density-independent factors hit a population whatever its size (a flood, a frost, a fire).

misconception.wrong: A population growing exponentially adds the same number of individuals every year.
misconception.right: It grows by the same percent every year, so the number added grows each year: 2% of 1,000 is 20, but 2% of 2,000 is 40.

summary: With unlimited resources, a population grows exponentially (a J-curve), by a constant percent each period. In real environments, limiting factors slow growth as the population nears carrying capacity, giving logistic growth (an S-curve). Density-dependent factors such as food shortage, disease and competition strengthen as a population grows; density-independent factors such as floods and frosts act whatever its size.
